articles.title: South Africa launched a €15-million programme to restore grasslands, savannas and thickets, with 100,000 hectares targeted by 2030
articles.summary: Rest of World News: South Africa has launched ReLISA, or Restoring Landscapes in South Africa, a 5-year, €15-million programme aimed at restoring degraded grassland, sava.
articles.body: South Africa has launched ReLISA, or Restoring Landscapes in South Africa, a 5-year, €15-million programme aimed at restoring degraded grassland, savanna and thicket ecosystems while expanding protected areas and strengthening climate and water resilience. The initiative is funded by Germany's Federal Ministry for the Environment through its International Climate Initiative and was jointly launched on October 16, 2025, on the sidelines of the G20 Environment and Climate Sustainability Working Group Ministerial Meeting in Cape Town. The launch brought together South Africa's Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, Dion George; Germany's Federal Minister for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety, Carsten Schneider; UNEP Deputy Executive Director Elizabeth Maruma Mrema; and UN Resident Coordinator in South Africa Nelson Muffuh. The programme is designed to connect ecological restoration with protected-area expansion, community partnerships and new approaches to financing conservation at landscape scale.Decades of land-use pressure have degraded key ecosystemsReLISA focuses on South Africa's Grassland, Savanna and Thicket Biomes, which EWT says have experienced decades of pressure from intensive land use. The organisation identifies overgrazing, mining, invasive alien plants, drought and fire among the factors contributing to degradation across these landscapes. Climate pressures are adding to those challenges through prolonged drought, high temperatures, wildfires and changing rainfall patterns.A particular focus is placed on Strategic Water Source Areas, or SWSAs. These landscapes are important for South Africa's water supply while also supporting agriculture, communities and biodiversity. EWT says degradation in these areas can affect water retention and erosion, while restoration can contribute to improved ecosystem resilience. The programme therefore links habitat restoration with broader goals around water security, climate adaptation and the livelihoods that depend on healthy landscapes.The programme brings together conservation, science and development organisationsReLISA is being implemented by a consortium that includes the United Nations Environment Programme, Endangered Wildlife Trust, United Nations Development Programme, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, C4 EcoSolutions and Unique Landuse. The programme's approach combines ecological restoration with economic valuation, financial innovation and collaboration with communities and land users.Within the programme, EWT is working in 3 target landscapes: the Northern Drakensberg, Soutpansberg and Amatholes. Field officers in these areas work with land users on rangeland management, ecological restoration and invasive alien plant clearing. The organisation says the work is intended not simply to increase the amount of protected land, but to strengthen connections between important wildlife corridors, intact habitat and properties containing threatened species.ReLISA aims to have 100,000 hectares under restoration by 2030One of the programme's central targets is to have 100,000 hectares across its key landscapes under restoration by 2030. The target covers landscapes considered important for biodiversity, water supply and climate resilience.The programme also includes plans to expand protected areas through biodiversity stewardship mechanisms. In the Northern Drakensberg, EWT says it is in the very early stages of establishing a proposed biosphere reserve focused on grassland habitat and existing protected-area networks along the northeastern escarpment between Royal Natal National Park and Memel in the eastern Free State. The proposal is part of a broader effort to connect conservation areas rather than treating individual protected sites as isolated units. The restoration target should not be interpreted as 100,000 hectares already restored. It is a target for the amount of land the programme aims to bring under restoration by 2030.New financing models are central to the restoration strategyReLISA is also intended to address one of the persistent challenges facing large-scale restoration: securing long-term financing. EWT says the programme is developing bankable business models designed to attract impact investors, agribusinesses and other private-sector participants to nature-based solutions. Potential mechanisms include payments for ecosystem services, carbon-focused finance through carbon credits and water-fund arrangements. The objective is to connect the ecological value of restoration with financial models that can support conservation work beyond individual grants or short-term projects.This approach builds on the idea that restoration can provide benefits beyond biodiversity. EWT identifies potential gains including improved water security, soil stabilisation, restored carbon stocks and stronger ecosystem resilience, while also linking healthier landscapes to agriculture, tourism and local livelihoods. These are intended outcomes of the programme rather than results that have already been demonstrated by ReLISA.The programme is intended to inform wider restoration effortsReLISA also has a policy and knowledge-sharing component. EWT says the programme will work with government partners on policy development and share lessons from its restoration work nationally and internationally. The stated aim is to help develop a longer-term restoration economy in South Africa by combining ecological work with community involvement and sustainable financing.The programme was officially launched during South Africa's 2025 G20 Environment and Climate Sustainability Working Group Ministerial Meeting in Cape Town. South Africa's Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment recorded the launch as part of the ministerial meeting's October 16 activities and described ReLISA as a partnership with Germany and UNEP focused on rehabilitating degraded land, creating jobs and building climate resilience. Its 2030 target now provides a measurable framework for the programme: bringing 100,000 hectares under restoration while testing ways to connect ecological recovery, protected-area expansion, water security and private investment across some of South Africa's degraded landscapes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sister of missing DC mom speaks out after ex’s arrest exposes 'horrifying' abusive relationship
articles.summary: Antoinette Forbes’ former partner was arrested last week, but authorities have not confirmed whether his case is connected to her disappearance.
articles.body: The sister of missing D.C. mother Antoinette Forbes revealed that she was unaware Antoinette had been in an abusive relationship until details of a 2021 assault surfaced following the arrest of the father of her 10-year-old son. Russell Ashford, 65, who was detained last week in Pennsylvania, reportedly took unauthorized overnight custody of their son on the night Antoinette was last seen, according to the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office. He also allegedly violated his probation stemming from the 2021 assault case, the office said. Authorities did not name Ashford as a suspect in Antoinette's disappearance. "Antoinette did not tell us at all about the assault in 2021, so just wrapping our minds around that, it's unfathomable. We can't really conceive it," Antoinette’s sister, Aileen, said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "I didn't hear about them until I saw some excerpts of the report after my sister went missing." FAMILY OF CRITICALLY MISSING DC MOTHER SAYS POLICE STILL TREATING HOME AS ACTIVE CRIME SCENE According to Maryland court filings, Ashford pleaded guilty to first-degree assault in 2021. During an argument over their child's schooling, Ashford allegedly threw Antoinette against the staircase, repeatedly punched her while she was lying on the kitchen floor and banged her head against the ground at least a dozen times until she lost consciousness, according to court filings. The assault continued until a neighbor heard her screaming and entered the home to intervene. After Antoinette was taken to a hospital, tests showed she suffered multiple facial lacerations, multiple fractured facial bones, eye damage, a concussion, a broken finger and bruising, court documents said. Prosecutors said the assault left Antoinette with permanent eye and hand injuries. After pleading guilty, Ashford was sentenced to 15 years in prison but served only nine months and five years' probation upon release, authorities said. Aileen said the reports came as a shock to her and her family, who are still processing the revelation. "The report is horrifying. And to tell the truth, I haven't had the time to fully process that. Just the thought of my sister enduring such a brutal attack is just deeply hurtful to me and to the rest of my family. We don't want to, we can't even conceive of it," Aileen said. FEDS PLAN NEW BAHAMAS SEARCH FOR LYNETTE HOOKER AFTER GPS DATA ALLEGEDLY TORPEDOES HUSBAND’S STORY: SOURCE Aileen noted that Antoinette may have kept the abuse from her family because she was protective of the people she loved. "Antoinette, she wanted to protect us from it. She did not want us to have any involvement with Russell," Aileen said. More than two weeks have passed since Antoinette was last seen on Friday, Sept. 4, just one week before she planned to take her son to visit their relatives in California, Aileen said. Antoinette was reported missing on Sept. 6 after friends found her dog, car, phone and wallet inside the home, but no sign of her. Shortly after her disappearance, Ashford was arrested for allegedly violating his probation, which strictly prohibited him from having hostile contact with Antoinette or their child, amid the concerning circumstances surrounding Antoinette's disappearance, court documents said. On July 16, 2026, Ashford reportedly arrived unannounced at his son's summer camp, but staff informed him he was not on the approved pickup list and asked for identification. Ashford allegedly became agitated and forceful with a counselor, prompting staff to file a formal written report about the incident. Pennsylvania State Police told Fox News Digital that Ashford was arrested after a traffic stop revealed he had an active warrant tied to the July incident. Authorities told Fox News Digital last week that the search for Antoinette is ongoing and that officials do not have any updates to share with the public. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Aileen further urged anyone living in the Nebraska Avenue Northwest neighborhood where Antoinette lived to check their security cameras and think back to anything that may have seemed peculiar. "Just check it, try to jog your memory," Aileen pleaded. "Was there something that seemed peculiar that might be something that you can come forward with and offer a detail to the authorities? It might make a difference." "To everyone who has been following this devastating story and who has been a part of the search for Antoinette, who showed up at the vigil, who's contributed to our GoFundMe account… I just want to say a deep thank you because it's so meaningful to me and our family."

articles.title: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
articles.summary: The UK has proposed handing the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and paying to lease back an important military base.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time.

Trump said UK-US relations are "more up now" that Burnham is in power, following their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Speaking to reporters, Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump and they had "taken that further today" following discussions on issues such as trade and immigration.

But the US president made clear his opposition to the UK's "terrible" deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back a joint UK-US military base on the archipelago's largest island, Diego Garcia.

Burnham, asked by broadcasters if the deal is "dead", later said the UK will "work hard" to find a resolution between the different sides and he is "confident we can find it working with our US partners".

Trump and Burnham met on Tuesday as they attended the United Nations for the annual gathering of world leaders.

Following bilateral talks, Burnham sat alongside Trump and used his opening remarks to say: "You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions and we've taken that further today."

The two men then faced questions shouted from the assembled press pack.

Asked by the BBC if Burnham was a man he could do business with, Trump said: "Yeah I do, I think he's a natural businessperson, we've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting we've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone.

"Yeah, I think so, he gets it, he understands what he has to do."

Burnham later said he had explained to Trump that Britain has been in "too much turbulence" in recent times but it is time to "turn the story" about the country into a positive one.

The US president added that the UK is a country with "great patriotism", and he thinks it is "waiting for good leadership, waiting for success".

Relations between Sir Keir and Trump also began well before becoming increasingly strained earlier this year when the then-prime minister refused to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran.

Trump reiterated his criticism of the Chagos Islands deal and stressed how a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia is "strategically very important", particularly in relation to US operations in Iran.

The agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back the military base - but in April the deal was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]."

He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".

Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well.

"What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."

The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who has long been a critic of the deal, posted on X: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."

Burnham also referenced that his private discussions with Trump included the Falkland Islands, which have been the subject of comments by the US president and Argentina's president Javier Milei.

The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.

Earlier this month, Trump hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the British overseas territory.

He had previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.

During a national address in early September, Milei also said: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".

Burnham told broadcasters: "We will stand firm in the face of any threats, we will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British.

"And I just wanted the [US] president to know directly from me, that's the clear British position, and he very much understood what I was saying."

One of the areas Burnham has been keen to focus on during his trip to the UN is artificial intelligence (AI).

The prime minister met business leaders, including Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook, on Tuesday.

He told them he wants a "single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks".

Burnham's approach could cause friction with Trump, with the president using his address to the UN General Assembly to say that the US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI.

Trump dubbed AI as "super intelligence" and said the US will "encourage it, not rein it in".

Burnham later met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with the PM apologising for arriving around 10 minutes late due to his bilateral with Trump running over.

Von der Leyen reassured the PM, saying: "These things are understandable."

articles.title: AOC opens up about race, gender in weighing possible 2028 White House bid
articles.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., opened up about how race and gender factor into her 2028 presidential election calculus in a new interview.
articles.body: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid. "Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times. "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities." The progressive congresswoman said of a possible White House run, "I think about it personally." "I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life," she added. AOC, ASKED ABOUT RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS HER AMBITION IS 'WAY BIGGER THAN THAT' "This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?" she told the Times. "That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism." Ocasio-Cortez said the discussion around race and gender was often seen as a complaint or excuse. "I often hesitate to even talk about it," she told the outlet, "because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint." "If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh," she told the Times of possibly running for president. "It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?" HASAN PIKER BRUSHES OFF DEMS WHO SEE HIM AS A LIABILITY, NAMES HIS '28 CHOICE She argued people get defensive when gender is suggested as playing a role in electoral politics. "I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left," she told the Times. Ocasio-Cortez has been generating 2028 buzz. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman described the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic." Hoffman made the comments at Politico's Decoded Summit in September, and said former Vice President Kamala Harris would have a "very challenging path" to the nomination. "It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for." AOC’S PRIMARY WIN REIGNITES SPECULATION OVER 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SCHUMER CHALLENGE Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said he would absolutely campaign for AOC should she decide to run in 2028. Ocasio-Cortez topped a July poll from the University of New Hampshire Granite State. In the poll, AOC was one point ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and 17 points ahead of Harris. The polling average as of Sept. 22, according to the New York Times, has Harris leading with 27%, followed by Gov. Gavin Newsom at 16%, Buttigieg with 10%, and Ocasio-Cortez also at 10%. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Judy Pino, advisor on Hispanic issues and a Spanish-language spokesperson for Independent Women and The LIBRE Initiative, reacted to Ocasio-Cortez' remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital. Pino said, "Whether America is ready for a Latina president isn’t the question. As a Latina, I find that framing beside the point and, frankly, insulting." "It reduces a serious debate about the future of this country to gender and ethnicity when Americans are worried about whether they can afford groceries, buy a home, grow a business, and create a better future for their children," she continued. Pino said Ocasio-Cortez "identifies" with democratic socialism, and argued, "we should believe candidates when they tell us what they stand for." "For many Latinos, that debate has particular resonance. Families from Cuba, Venezuela and elsewhere in Latin America have witnessed governments embrace socialism while expanding state control and restricting economic and political freedom. Those experiences help explain why the word ‘socialism’ can carry consequences far beyond a political slogan for some Latino families,' Pino said in the statement. Pino said Latino voters were more focused on AOC's policies rather than her gender or ethnicity. "That's the debate America should be having: not whether we're ready for a Latina president, but whether Americans want to move this country in a socialist direction," she said.

articles.title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
articles.summary: The defence deal signed at the UN General Assembly also re-affirms Denmark's sovereignty over its semi-autonomous Arctic territory.
articles.body:
The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it.

At a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations".

Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win".

The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory.

Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth.

His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral".

The deal signed on Tuesday amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US.

The new agreement says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east.

Narsarsuaq has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were surveying last week, according to Danish media.

The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit.

The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties.

Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there.

It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland".

Speaking at the signing ceremony, Trump said: "We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship."

"This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible."

Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation".

"Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever."

The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination".

Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us.

"It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country.

"Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation.

The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark.

The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base.

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.

He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks.

However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal.

The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles.

Trump said last week that the new deal came with "no cost to the United States".

A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".

articles.title: US signs ‘tremendous’ Arctic security deal with Denmark, Greenland
articles.summary: NATO and the European Union welcome accord that ends months-long standoff after Trump threatened to seize Greenland.
articles.body:
The United States, Denmark and Greenland have signed a deal on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, granting Washington a greater military presence on the continent-sized Arctic island.

After years of tensions between the US and Denmark, which holds sovereignty over the autonomous and resource-rich territory of Greenland, Tuesday’s agreement resolves a key point of contention among Western transatlantic allies. It is set to expand a longstanding US presence just as great-power competition with Russia and China heats up.

“This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States and for everybody,” US President Donald Trump said before signing the agreement. “And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible.”

Addressing the UNGA earlier on Tuesday, Trump said the US would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations”, including “building two very major military bases”.

The agreement allows Washington to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base in northwest Greenland. Bases will be established at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east with the option to “establish additional defense areas” and expand operations.

It also permits US aircraft to fly over and land anywhere in Greenland, including its territorial waters while also granting “undersea access”.

No non-NATO country will be allowed to set up military installations or a “persistent” military presence in Greenland without unanimous approval by Denmark, Greenland and the US. The agreement also bars investors from “sensitive sectors” outside NATO and the European Union.

The accord does not have an end date. If Greenland becomes independent, it will remain in NATO and assume Denmark’s obligations under the deal.

“The Danish government and the Greenland government will maintain sovereignty over Greenland’s territory, but the US will have essentially veto power over what other countries are able to come to the island,” said Al Jazeera correspondent Rosiland Jordan reporting from UN Headquarters in New York.

“It does give Washington a great deal of what it wants: a military presence and the ability to keep rival nations, notably China and Russia, off,” she added.

The deal follows a months-long standoff after Trump threatened to seize Greenland, prompting warnings from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen that a US takeover would end the NATO alliance.

Since 1945, the US military presence in Greenland shrank from thousands of troops across 17 bases to about 200 stationed at the remote Pituffik base.

Frederiksen called the new agreement “a deal that can last forever”, while Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described it as “a win-win-win”, saying: “Your security is our security, and our security is your security.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European Council President Antonio Costa both welcomed the deal, with the latter calling it “a positive step for transatlantic cooperation and Arctic security”, grounded in “respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.

articles.title: Qatar’s emir urges diplomacy as Gulf at ‘one of the most dangerous phases’
articles.summary: Sheikh Tamim says years of delayed diplomacy led to the US-Israel war on Iran.
articles.body:
The Gulf is experiencing “one of the most dangerous phases” due to the US-Israel war on Iran that “can be resolved through diplomatic means”, Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has said at the United Nations General Assembly.

Reaffirming Qatar’s role as a “trusted mediator”, Sheikh Tamim said on Tuesday that diplomacy would lead to a lasting solution ensuring security for the entire region, including Iran.

“We remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war,” Sheikh Tamim said, in translated remarks.

Qatar is doing “everything in our power to address the conflict in the region through diplomatic means” but remains “steadfast” in defending its territory and sovereignty, he said.

Shortly after Sheikh Tamim’s address, United States President Donald Trump said officials held a “very good” three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation. Prior to the meeting, Trump repeated threats to “annihilate” Iran in his UN speech.

Sheikh Tamim said the war on Iran was the “cumulative result of years” of postponing diplomatic resolutions and called for a “regional system of collective security”.

“In the absence of such a system, it has become possible for a war to erupt,” he said.

Sheikh Tamim slammed Israel for its “aggression” in the occupied West Bank and Gaza, saying attacks have expanded to neighbouring countries, “affecting the security of the region as a whole”.

“There can be no talk of a just international order as long as Palestine remains in its plight,” he said. “What has transpired in Gaza is genocide in every sense of the word.”

Sheikh Tamim expressed Qatar’s support for Lebanon, Sudan and Libya, calling for state sovereignty.

“We support United Nations efforts aimed at reaching a comprehensive political settlement based on the outcomes of the national dialogue facilitated by the United Nations, in a manner that preserves Yemen’s unity and sovereignty and achieves security and stability,” he said.

The speech comes as the nearly seven-month-old war increasingly threatens the Gulf’s economic lifelines, with the US and Iran trading strikes on oil tankers and other vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

In September, Saudi Arabia shuttered the key East-West oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq.

Meanwhile, a new spell of fighting has broken out in Yemen, following territorial advances by the Houthi rebel group towards the critical Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The war began after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28 amid negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme, killing its supreme leader, other top officials and dozens of civilians.

Iran responded by launching strikes across the Gulf region, including the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain.

articles.title: Spain clears way for US extradition case against  millionaire activist
articles.summary: The Spanish cabinet has allowed a US extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers, an American millionaire and Gaza donor, to proceed to Spanish courts.
articles.body: The Spanish cabinet has allowed a US extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers, an American millionaire and Gaza donor, to proceed to Spanish courts in a decision that his lawyers warn will set a “dangerous precedent” for the defense of the Palestinian cause in Europe. The Council of Ministers’ decision clears the way for the case to move into its judicial phase, a stage that brings Chambers’ potential extradition one step closer. On July 10, Spanish officers in unmarked police vehicles arrested Chambers on the Spanish island of Ibiza as he and his partner drove with their son to look at schools. His arrest followed the issuance of an Interpol Red Notice at the request of the United States, according to his lawyer, Baltasar Garzón. Chambers, 41, is an heir to a slice of the Cox Media fortune who cashed out three years ago for a reported $250 million. He’s long been a supporter of Palestinian human rights. Spain’s current government too has been a fierce critic of how Israel has prosecuted its war in Gaza – calling it a genocide, imposing an arms embargo and recognising the state of Palestine, leading to rocky relations with the United States. Chambers’ critics point to his online support for the Hamas-led October 7 attacks, as well as his anti-American rhetoric – including calling the US the “Great Satan.” He has been held since his arrest at the Aranjuez prison near Madrid and has lodged an asylum claim in Spain. The indictment against Chambers is sealed, but his lawyer tells CNN that US prosecutors have charged him with money laundering – including transferring more than $7.5 million to a Tunisian football team – and with riot and conspiracy to riot, tied to 2023 protests at an Israeli arms manufacturer’s US facilities in New Hampshire and Massachusetts. Chambers’ lawyers say the charges are politically motivated. “We must respect the decision of the Council of Ministers. However, it sets a dangerous precedent regarding the defense of the Palestinian cause,” Garzón said in a statement shared with CNN following the cabinet’s decision Tuesday. Garzón previously represented WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange alongside Chambers’ US attorney, Barry Pollack. “Spain cannot defend international law, the rights of the Palestinian people and those who provide humanitarian aid while at the same time allowing a request to proceed with an extradition that shows clear signs of political persecution,” Garzón added. Garzón said Chambers has given much of his fortune away to humanitarian projects in Gaza, including a bakery, a community kitchen, mobile clinics and reconstructive surgery for children wounded in the war. Garzón said the Tunisia transfer, made while Chambers was living there, paid off a struggling football club’s debt and covered salaries, plus personal expenses, which he argued isn’t money laundering under Spanish law since the funds weren’t illegally sourced. Four people who took part in the New Hampshire protest were sentenced to 60 days each in prison, while Chambers faces up to five years if convicted of riot and conspiracy to riot over the same episode. Garzón contends that his client wasn’t even in Massachusetts when the protest took place, but was in Atlanta, Georgia. The lawyer cited the Trump administration’s 2025 ICC-related sanctions measures and a broader NGO-funding memo, alongside Human Rights Watch reporting on US sanctions imposed later that year on several Palestinian rights groups, as context for his claim of political persecution of his client. Relations between the Trump administration and the government of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez have been tense in recent months, with US President Donald Trump critical of Sánchez’s opposition to the war in Iran and of the country’s handling of immigration. The left-wing Sumar coalition, part of Spain’s governing alliance, had urged the government to block the extradition. “The extradition amounts to the criminalization of solidarity with Palestine,” said Enrique Santiago, Sumar’s deputy parliamentary spokesperson. Ione Belarra, a member of Spain’s Congress of Deputies and secretary-general of the left-wing Podemos party, called Chambers “the first political prisoner in Spanish history being imprisoned because of his support for Palestine.” “The government has done what it is required to do at this stage, something that is purely procedural,” said government spokesperson Elma Saiz, who added that Chambers will have “all the necessary safeguards” during the National Court’s review of the extradition request. “We must now let the National Court and Mr. Chambers’ defense team do their work, and once the National Court’s ruling is known, with all the arguments on the table, a final decision will be made,” Saiz added. CNN has reached out to the US Department of Justice for comment. Chambers’ partner, US actress Stella Schnabel, is three months pregnant with their second child. “Fergie could spend the first year of our child’s life unable to hold them, seeing them only through a pane of glass, despite not being convicted of any crime,” she said in a written statement provided to CNN. “Fergie should be with me and our children, continuing his philanthropy, not sitting in a prison cell because of it.”

articles.title: A gold-domed New York City penthouse first listed for $25 million has sold for $9 million after 530 days on the market, with owner Greg Carr directing the sale proceeds to his conservation project
articles.summary: US News: A historic Manhattan penthouse set inside a gold leaf dome has sold at auction for $9 million, ending a 530 day stretch on the market that saw its ori.
articles.body: A historic Manhattan penthouse set inside a gold leaf dome has sold at auction for $9 million, ending a 530 day stretch on the market that saw its original asking price cut by 64 percent. The landmark home atop the historic Sohmer Piano Building in the Flatiron District was first listed for $25 million in November 2024 by technology entrepreneur and philanthropist Greg Carr. After failing to find a buyer through traditional channels, the unit was sold through Concierge Auctions as part of its live "America 250" sale in New York City, according to real estate reporting by the New York Post and CityRealty. Carr, a co-founder of Boston Technology, pledged to send all net proceeds from the sale to the Gorongosa Project, a conservation effort focused on restoring Mozambique's Gorongosa National Park and supporting the surrounding communities.A landmark architectural footprintThe penthouse sits atop the 13-story Beaux-Arts Sohmer Piano Building at 170 Fifth Avenue, originally designed in the 1890s by architect Robert Maynicke. Spanning about 5,777 square feet across two main levels, the home has five bedrooms and four and a half bathrooms. The apartment's standout feature is its octagonal gilded dome, which holds a two-story private room with 360-degree views across Manhattan, including landmarks like the Flatiron Building, Madison Square Park, and the Empire State Building. Inside, the home features wide white oak floors, tall ceilings, 40 oversized windows, and a grand limestone staircase beneath an 80-foot glass skylight. The upper floor opens onto a private rooftop terrace with a fire pit for outdoor dining. Public property records cited by CityRealty show that Carr originally bought the duplex penthouse in 2007 for $7.22 million.Funding wildlife conservation in AfricaCarr has spent more than two decades putting his personal fortune toward philanthropy following his success in the tech industry. Through his foundation, he has personally committed more than $100 million to habitat restoration, wildlife protection, and community development programs in Mozambique. Explaining his decision to sell the Manhattan property, Carr pointed to his changing routine and work commitments overseas. "I work in Africa, and I go home for holidays in Idaho," Carr told reporters, as cited in marketing coverage published by property blog Francis York, "so it wasn't leaving a lot of time for New York." Listing details provided by Sotheby's International Realty agents Claire Groome and Lawrence Treglia, who co-marketed the home alongside Concierge Auctions, confirmed the auction bidding closed on July 29, 2026, landing the final sale price at $9 million.Auction dynamics in the Manhattan luxury marketThe steep price cut reflects wider shifts in Manhattan's high-end property market, where unique or highly customized luxury homes often sit on the market for a long time before reaching a realistic price through competitive bidding. By taking the property to live auction, the seller secured a firm sale after 530 days of a static listing, freeing up funds for the ongoing conservation projects in Africa. The identity of the buyer who purchased the gold-domed penthouse has not yet been made public in official deed transfer records.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ICE officer who shot man in Austin was issued a body cam but wasn’t wearing it
articles.summary: The officer was issued a body camera but officials said it was not clear why he was not wearing it. Another officer’s body cam only captured partial footage of the shooting.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News. The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back. On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone. After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene. Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting. The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said. The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements. Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed. Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.” He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said. “Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post. Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain. “We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.” The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain. “He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said. “We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.” Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.” He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release. A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S. A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney. On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.” Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop. ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras. A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car. “I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades. “You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said. A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side. At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection. Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around. The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming. The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole. An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle. “This is unjust,” she says as she’s recording the video. Julia Ainsley reported from Washington, D.C., Daniella Silva from New York and Albinson Linares from Austin, Texas.

articles.title: Man scales locked gate in chilling video after allegedly chasing college student home, then walks free: police
articles.summary: Security video shows a man scaling a locked gate to follow a UC Berkeley student into her apartment complex after allegedly chasing her home.
articles.body: Chilling surveillance video shows a UC Berkeley student racing through a locked gate as a homeless man allegedly chased her home, only to watch him scale the barrier, enter her apartment complex and remain free while prosecutors decide whether to charge him. The frightening Sept. 15 encounter was captured on security video outside the apartment building in Berkeley, California. The video shows the woman entering the secured complex around 8 p.m. Seconds later, a man climbs over the locked gate and allegedly follows her inside while holding an object initially reported as a knife. VIRAL VIDEO OF HOMELESS ENCAMPMENT AROUND CITY OF BERKELEY SPARKS SAFETY CONCERNS FROM PARENT Berkeley police later determined the object was likely a barbecue lighter and said there was no direct contact between the man and the woman. The student, identified only as Eden for safety reasons, told ABC7 she had been walking her dog on Berkeley Way when the man made strange gestures, approached her and then began running toward her. She made it inside the complex and reached an elevator before he could see where she went, according to the outlet. "I shut the gate behind me, heard him and saw him climbing the gate," Eden told ABC7. UCLA SORORITIES HIRE PRIVATE SECURITY AMID TERRIFYING HARASSMENT BY HOMELESS MEN: REPORT The Berkeley Police Department said it received the woman’s call at approximately 8:04 p.m. Patrol officers were handling other high-priority emergencies at the time, including a domestic violence case and a report involving a missing person considered at risk. Eden told ABC7 that officers arrived about an hour later but were unable to locate the man. The next night, at approximately 9:24 p.m., police received another call reporting that the same man was lying on a sidewalk near Berkeley Way and Walnut Street. Officers responded, detained and identified him, according to the department. Police confirmed that he was the person involved in the previous night’s alleged trespassing but did not arrest him. FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS The department said California law generally prevents officers from making a warrantless arrest for a misdemeanor that did not occur in their presence. Because the alleged trespassing had happened the day before, officers said they could not arrest the man based solely on that offense. Instead, investigators submitted the case to the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office for review. Prosecutors will determine whether criminal charges should be filed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP ABC7 reported that the district attorney’s office confirmed it was reviewing the case and that no charges had been filed as of Monday. Eden said she was stunned a man could allegedly chase her into a secured building and still walk away after police identified him. She called for stronger laws and greater protections for residents, according to the outlet. UC Berkeley and the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

articles.title: Simone Biles says three masked men burglarized her home and stole her car
articles.summary: Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles is down one luxury car and up one security dog after three masked men stole her Porsche GTS, she told her TikTok followers on Monday.
articles.body: Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles is down one luxury car and up one security dog after three masked men stole her Porsche GTS, she told her TikTok followers on Monday. “Get ready with me to pick up my new car,” the gymnast said with an upbeat squeal as she applied makeup in her bathroom. Biles, 29, said the robbery happened during her last months in Chicago and is partially responsible for why she and her husband, Jonathan Owens, now have a Dobermann Pinscher. “I feel like I need a reality TV show,” Biles said. “The things that happen to me are absolute insanity.” Chicago police said it could not provide an incident report to NBC News. In recent years, several high-profile athletes across multiple sports have reported home break-ins and robberies. Kansas City Chiefs players Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce were both robbed in October 2024. The homes of basketball pros Sabrina Ionescu of the New York Liberty and Karl-Anthony Towns of the New York Knicks were robbed in 2025. The home of Shedeur Sanders of the Cleveland Browns was robbed by four men as he played a game earlier this year. Biles said her old car was recovered but she and Owens, a safety for the Indianapolis Colts, decided to get a new one anyway: “When they turned that thing on, I was sold,” she said. The world’s most decorated gymnast made headlines in June when she revealed on social media that she almost died, though she did not share the circumstances. “I’m not one to normally share things like this because I value privacy in today’s age,” Biles said in a post, “but almost dying wasn’t on my bingo card earlier this week.”

articles.title: North Korean defector issues stark warning about America ahead of Christian university's anti-communism event
articles.summary: Cornerstone University's anti-communist event features North Korean defector Yeonmi Park and Cultural Revolution survivor Xi Van Fleet speaking.
articles.body: Cornerstone University, a Christian school in Michigan, is holding an anti-communist event, bringing in scholars and survivors of oppressive regimes. Dr. Gerson Moreno-Riaño, the president of Cornerstone University, said the school chose the theme months ago, as it saw public opinion across the country sway toward communism and socialism. The Oct. 1 event is titled, "Why Not Communism? A Wisdom Conversation on Freedom, Faith and the Future of America." "Frankly, we became alarmed and concerned because the history of communism, socialism is a dark one," Moreno-Riaño told Fox News Digital. OPINION: WANT TO STOP SOCIALISM? A MODERN CIVIC EDUCATION NEEDS A LOT MORE THAN YOU'D THINK "We thought we need to step up as a university committed to educating men and women for our country and really inform the community, educate the community and our students and the country at large about the moral bankruptcy of communism and socialism," he added. The university is located in Grand Rapids, Michigan, which sits in Kent County, an area where Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed won more than 61% of the vote in the primary, according to state records. El-Sayed famously campaigned with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who defended communism as the "honorable end goal" of socialism, giving the event added relevance. The event speakers include Babylon Bee CEO Seth Dillon; Dr. Gary Saul Morson, a scholar of Soviet communism; Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution survivor Xi Van Fleet, and North Korean defector Yeonmi Park. "Yeonmi Park's story is incredible, as a defector of North Korea. Xi Van Fleet, her time in a labor camp in China. And what they saw, what they experienced, what they witnessed is absolutely essential, because there are certain similarities between what happened in North Korea and is happening there now, what happened in China during Mao Zedong and thereafter, similarities between what happens there in those revolutions and what's happening here has been happening here for several years," Moreno-Riaño said. HASAN PIKER VOWS NEVER TO CRITICIZE MAO ZEDONG IN RESURFACED VIDEO, HAILS HIM AS ‘GREAT LEADER’ Park told Fox News Digital that communism is on the rise among students who learn about it "in a very nice classroom with the air conditioning running," while she experienced oppressive regimes firsthand. "I had to live through [a] real socialist government every day until I escaped from North Korea," Park said. "And I know it is not nice when it is actually enforced [in] real life. Many people think it's [an] amazing thing as a theory, and they have no idea if we do bring this policy in our government, what that's going to [do to] our local population." Growing up in North Korea during the devastating famines of the 1990s, Park experienced hunger, severe poverty and political persecution. At age 13, she escaped with her mother across the frozen border river into China, where they experienced human trafficking. After her mother submitted to sexual assault to protect Yeonmi from smugglers, both were sold into trafficking rings. After two years of exploitation and hiding from Chinese authorities, Christian activist networks helped them cross from China to Mongolia, where they secured political asylum, and later gained their freedom in South Korea. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE REAL REASON COMMUNISTS FEAR RELIGION AND WANT BELIEVERS SILENCED Park told Fox News Digital that while in the U.S. she has had students who are unaware of her background tell her that she does not "understand oppression" because she is Asian. Park added that they refer to her as a "White-passing person." "They have no idea that I was, at 13 years old, being sold as a sex slave in China for two years of my life. I do understand oppression," she said. Park insisted that American students often take their freedom for granted and do not have a full understanding of global realities. "Most people are not free right now in the world. More than 70% of humanity right now live under authoritarian governments," Park told Fox News Digital, likely referencing data from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute. V-Dem's most recent report estimates that 74% of the world's population lives under autocracies. She added that having freedom is "a very special thing" and she doesn't "want us to lose this amazing country, because if America falls, we do not have a place to escape to." "For me, I was fortunate that I had a country to escape to from North Korea to America, but if we lose this country, we are all going to die, actually," she said. SEN TOM COTTON: DEMOCRATS SAY SOCIALISM WILL HELP. HISTORY SAYS IT WILL HURT For Moreno-Riaño, the defense of freedom is directly tied to Cornerstone University's Christian identity. He explained to Fox News Digital that the principle of liberty was, in his view, "at the bedrock" of the Christian faith. "I mean, we believe that the gospel sets us free. So, liberty and freedom are at the core of our Christian faith through the gospel of Jesus Christ," he said. "We believe this basic Christian principle called the Imago Dei, that we've been created in His image, means that for us to flourish, you have to have a condition of freedom and liberty. It's absolutely essential," he added. Ultimately, Moreno-Riaño hopes to encourage students to take action and to resist the urge to "sit on the sidelines watching." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "As people of faith, Christians here at Cornerstone University, we want our students to be involved to be great citizens, modeling their faith and modeling what it means to be a great citizen of our great country. That to me is the ultimate outcome for not just the students, but even for the community at large who will come to the event," he said.

articles.title: US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
articles.summary: The delivery driver was transferred from a hospital to a detention centre after the shooting on Sunday.
articles.body:
A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said it is investigating the shooting of an illegal migrant in the Texan capital, but have not confirmed he was shot in the back.

It comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.

Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer

Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.

Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.

"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.

"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."

The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.

A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.

Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.

He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.

Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.

Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.

Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.

Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.

The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.

He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

articles.title: Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘supporting’ Hamas ahead of UN visit: ‘Shame on you’
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday accused New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) of “supporting” the terror group Hamas ahead of visiting the United Nations General Assembly in the city. “Shame on you, Mr. Mamdani,” Netanyahu said in a video posted to the social platform X. “Shame on you for supporting the Hamas…
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday accused New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) of “supporting” the terror group Hamas ahead of visiting the United Nations General Assembly in the city.

“Shame on you, Mr. Mamdani,” Netanyahu said in a video posted to the social platform X . “Shame on you for supporting the Hamas terrorist monsters who butchered our people. Shame on you for inciting riots against New York Jews.”

Netanyahu said he was heading for the U.N. to “tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I’m going to tell the truth about you.” The video’s release came when Mamdani, after meeting with President Trump at the mayor’s home Gracie Mansion on Monday, called the prime minister a “war criminal” in an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour.

Mamdani responded to Netanyahu’s message, saying at a press conference that what the prime minister said “in that video is not true,” Politico reported . He accused Netanyahu of being “the architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians.”

“What we do know to actually be the truth when it comes to the prime minister is that he is the subject of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity,” Mamdani added.

Mamdani has repeatedly condemned the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and has denied accusations of antisemitism from Republican and some Democratic critics. Netanyahu has dismissed accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity , charges that are the basis of the ICC’s arrest warrant from November 2024.

The mayor floated the idea of adhering to the ICC arrest warrant and having Netanyahu detained during his visit to the U.N. General Assembly. Mamdani later backed off his threat but urged the federal government to join the ICC and execute the warrant.

The U.S. and Israel are not subject to the ICC’s rulings, as neither country ratified the treaty that created the ICC, the Rome Statute, and therefore does not recognize the court’s jurisdiction over its citizens, service members or government officials.

But the ICC asserts jurisdiction over Palestinian territories and recognizes the state of Palestine as a party subject to the Rome Statute.

The prime minister has long been critical of the mayor, who campaigned last year by showing his support for Gaza’s Palestinian population and criticized the U.S. government’s closeness to the Israeli government.

“Look at what he’s doing. He’s fomenting hate,” Netanyahu told Fox News in July. “He’s supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers, Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone.”

The Israel-Hamas war has been on pause for almost one year since both sides agreed to a ceasefire, but Israel has continued to conduct strikes across the territory. About 1,200 Israelis were killed in the initial Hamas attack on Israel in 2023. Israeli attacks on the territory have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 1,300 since the ceasefire deal was reached, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
